newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-GEBRSELASSIE RETAINS TITLE WITH CONSUMMATE EASE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-GEBRSELASSIE RETAINS TITLE WITH CONSUMMATE EASE.

text.p: Long distance king Haile Gebrselassie won his third consecutive world title over 10,000 metres with consummate ease on Wednesday in a repeat of last year's Olympic final.
Gebrselassie made his decisive move with 600 metres remaining to clock 27 minutes 24.58 seconds as night fell on the packed Athens stadium.
Kenyan Paul Tergat came a distant second in 27:25.62 and Moroccan Salah Hissou was third in 27:28.67. The top three had finished in exactly the same order in Atlanta.
World record holder Gebrselassie had threatened not to come to Greece because he feared the track might be too hard and asked unsuccessfully for it to be watered.
At the Atlanta Olympics, he had sought a rare double but withdrew from the 5,000 metres after sustaining severe blisters from the hard track while winning the 10,000 metres.
"The track was a little better than I had expected, not quite as hard as the one in Atlanta," he said.
The 24-year-old from the Ethiopian village of Assela, set on a hill 3,000 metres above sea level, ran a faultless tactical race in his trademark, smooth style.
The diminutive Gebrselassie stayed just behind the leaders for most of the race, letting Kenyans Dominic Kirui and Paul Koech set the early pace.
Hissou, who briefly held the world record before Gebrselassie recaptured it last month in Oslo, seized the lead with eight laps remaining.
Then Koech tried his luck, running in front for the next few laps with Gebreselassie on his heels.
Halfway through the penultimate lap, the Ethiopian accelerated leaving his rivals helpless in his wake.
Tergat and Hissou followed as best they could while an exhausted Koech dropped off the pace to end up fourth.
"It's never easy to run in this sort of company," said Tergat.
Without taking time to catch his breath after crossing the line, Gebrselassie picked up an Ethiopian flag and embarked on a victory lap, which he completed at a brisk pace.
"I am not a person from another planet, I am a human being," he insisted shortly afterwards when asked about his awesome performance.
"I am proud to have won three world titles," he added, explaining he felt he did not have anything more to prove in world championships.
Gebrselassie might find it hard to set new goals after winning just about everything at stake but Hissou promised to keep him busy.
"I will attempt to break the world record in Brussels (on August 22)," he said.
Gebrselassie was not impressed.
"If somebody beats my world record, I will try to get it back," he said.
He appeared puzzled when someone asked him which bid he supported for the 2004 Olympics, in which he said he might enter the marathon.
"I'm in favour of Cape Town because Africa has never had the Olympics but I'd rather run in Stockholm," he said. "I'm a man of two cities."

Cape Town and Stockholm are in the final short list of five from which the International Olympic Committee will choose the host city in Lausanne next month. The other three are Rome, Athens and Buenos Aires.
